item.title: Rise of domestic brands reeling in 'China haul'
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Rise of domestic brands reeling in 'China haul' Mariana Rizzo, a 23-year-old Italian studying architecture at the University of Naples Federico II, has made shopping part of her experience of everyday life in China. She first visited the country in 2023 and has returned three times, with some trips lasting almost two months. Her shopping list includes beauty products, clothing, accessories, snacks, technology and lifestyle goods, as well as items that are harder to find in Italy. "When it comes to Chinese brands, one of the beauty brands I really like is Flower Knows. I love their makeup, but also the packaging and the attention they put into the design," she said. Rizzo is among the growing number of foreigners visiting the country for the "China haul" — a trend of international travelers filling their suitcases with Chinese products before heading home. Underpinning the phenomenon is the growing appreciation of the quality and modern appeal of Chinese brands often highlighted on social media and shopping platforms. "Sometimes I see something on Xiaohongshu or Douyin and think, 'I need to find this when I go to China!'" Rizzo said. "For me, shopping in China is not just about getting something cheaper. It's about having access to a much wider variety of products and experiencing the trends and lifestyle of the country directly," she said. Her favorite purchases include a qipao, the traditional dress worn by Chinese women, and a DJI Osmo Pocket 4 camera for recording her travels. "Buying it in China was particularly interesting because DJI is a Chinese technology brand, and I was able to discover and buy it directly there," said Rizzo, adding that the camera was considerably cheaper in China than in Italy. She has also noticed growing interest in Chinese products and brands among her friends and classmates in Italy, and sometimes she introduces them to brands she has discovered. A US tourist is measured for a custom-made suit at a clothing store in the South Bund Fabric Market in Shanghai on July 22. WANG XIANG/XINHUA Better than socks The appeal of homegrown Chinese brands among overseas shoppers is increasingly visible in Shanghai. Foreign customers accounted for about 35 percent of sales at footwear brand Pane's two Shanghai stores, while overseas shoppers accounted for around 30 percent of sales at Wangxiaoben's Shanghai stores, according to a report by Jiefang Daily in June. Wang Xianming, founder of Wangxiaoben, a Chinese lifestyle brand known for its bags, said the appeal lies in the happiness their products bring shoppers. When he established the brand in 2016, he started with socks, hoping to turn a basic necessity into an accessory that could lift people's mood. "I wanted socks to be more than just something people wear. They could also complement an outfit, express a sense of style and bring a little happiness to everyday life, even if only for 15 seconds," Wang said. In 2024, Wangxiaoben began making what Wang calls "dopamine" bags, which have since become its main product category. The brand's product range also includes hats, socks and pet accessories. Wang first noticed an increase in foreign customers in 2024, particularly visitors from Southeast Asia and Russia shopping at the company's store in Shanghai's Super Brand Mall. In September 2025 it opened a store at Shanghai Joy City and noticed South Korean and American bloggers sharing content about its products. "Online platforms in Thailand and Russia began working with us, making our products available to new consumers," said Wang of the overseas bloggers' brand promotions. One South Korean blogger, for example, posted a video of the brand's Shanghai store this summer, prompting numerous inquiries from her followers. She subsequently bought more than 100 bags for followers and friends during her stay in the city. Wangxiaoben products have also attracted repeat international shoppers. A Malaysian woman visited Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, three times over two years, buying multiple products on each trip and developing a close friendship with the store manager, Wang said. Customers from Southeast Asia tend to prefer lower-priced bags, while those from Japan and South Korea seem to care less about prices. The brand's overseas customers also span a wider age range than its younger Chinese shoppers. "We are not making major adjustments specifically for foreign customers. In Shanghai, we are looking into tax-refund policies and other measures to make shopping more convenient for international visitors," Wang said. Wangxiaoben has around 120 stores nationwide, mainly in tourist destinations and major cities such as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Nanjing in Jiangsu province, and Chengdu in Sichuan province. It has registered its trademarks overseas and plans to expand gradually into international markets through social media promotion, while exploring complementary products around the lifestyle concept behind its "dopamine" range. "I can clearly see that overseas consumers are developing greater trust in and appreciation for Chinese brands. This is closely related to the development of China's manufacturing, design and branding capabilities. It feels a little like how Chinese consumers once felt when they went abroad to buy local brands," said Wang. Premium goods Beyond individual shopping experiences, broader consumer perceptions of Chinese brands are evolving. According to Ipsos' 2025 Global Trust Index for Chinese Brands, the global net trust score for Chinese brands rose by 12 percentage points from the previous year to 32 percent, while the proportion of consumers in developed markets who expressed trust in Chinese brands reached 36 percent. Guo Xiaoling, a professor of marketing at the Business School of the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said Chinese brands must win acceptance, trust and even become aspirational for consumers in developed markets to command a price premium. "In the early 2000s, when China joined the World Trade Organization, 'Made in China' was often associated with low prices and value for money, targeting lower-end market segments rather than mainstream markets. Over the past two decades, China has made significant progress in the transition from Chinese products to Chinese brands," said Guo. Overseas perceptions of Chinese brands have been shaped by China's growing national strength and cultural influence, breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and new energy vehicles, as well as improvements in innovation, design, quality and sustainability, she said. Citing Bain & Company's 2025 China Personal Luxury Report, Guo pointed to homegrown high-end brands such as fashion label Icicle, jewelry brand Laopu Gold, fragrance brand Documents and handbag maker Songmont. "Brand craftsmanship, storytelling and interactions with potential consumers on social media now play a major role in stimulating consumer interest and desire," said Guo. At Songmont's flagship store at Indigo shopping mall in Beijing, she met young foreign consumers who had come specifically to shop and learned they had discovered the brand through social media. When teaching foreign exchange students, Guo asked them to visit well-known Chinese brand experience spaces, such as Pop Land. She believes these firsthand interactions deepen their understanding of Chinese brands and culture and encourage positive word-of-mouth when they return home. "If social media is the digital infrastructure for elevating Chinese brands, then firsthand experience is the booster and the experience capsule built on top of it," she said. Chinese businesses should recognize that their brands represent the country to overseas consumers, whether through Laopu Gold's cultural heritage or Pop Mart's broader appeal. "When overseas consumers learn that a brand they like originates in China, their fondness for that brand will inevitably lead to a more positive perception of Chinese brands as a whole," said Guo. A livestream host for a cross-border e-commerce platform showcases new jewelry collections at the Yiwu Global Digital Trade Center in Yiwu, Zhejiang province, ahead of this year's Singles Day shopping rush. LYU BIN/FOR CHINA DAILY Cross-border sales While overseas consumers are increasingly discovering Chinese products through travel and social media, Chinese e-commerce platforms are also stepping up efforts to reach them in their home markets. China's cross-border e-commerce imports and exports reached 2.84 trillion yuan in 2025, up 4.8 percent year-on-year, the General Administration of Customs said at a press conference in July. The challenge for Chinese businesses is turning overseas consumer interest into purchases and repeat business, with this year's overseas Singles Day shopping season already underway. AliExpress launched its sales campaign on Nov 1, with promotions running through Nov 18 before moving into its Black Friday campaign. According to AliExpress data, the volume of goods stocked in its overseas warehouses ahead of this year's Singles Day online shopping rush rose 146 percent year-on-year. George Wang, chief financial officer of Shoplazza, an AI-native e-commerce platform that has served more than 650,000 merchants worldwide, said merchants' priorities have shifted from simply setting up overseas online stores to learning how to operate and grow their businesses in international markets. "Acquiring customers online has become harder, so merchants have to watch spending, conversion and margins much more closely. Over the past two years, one clear trend is that merchants' needs are shifting from 'help me set up an overseas online store' to 'help me run my overseas business'," said Wang. "Social media helps consumers discover brands, and this sparks their interest, while content creators build trust through product reviews, demonstrations, and firsthand experiences," he said. Overseas consumers usually pass through several processes before buying, including watching a product video on social media, reading a creator's review, and comparing options on a marketplace or the brand's own website. "Some brands using Shoplazza's platform include links on their online stores that direct customers to Amazon, allowing consumers to choose their preferred purchasing channel. This approach lets the two channels work together, with the brand's own online store driving traffic to Amazon while helping merchants build lasting customer relationships through direct sales," said Wang. On Oct 5, TikTok announced an AI shopping assistant and Buy Direct, a one-click checkout tool, with partners including Shoplazza. "The shopping assistant allows consumers to ask about sizing, product details, delivery and stock before proceeding to the checkout, without leaving the TikTok app," he said. Wang gave the example of Real-SilkLife, a Chinese direct-to-consumer brand offering silk, cashmere and linen clothing and home products, primarily in the US and Europe. By using Shoplazza's system and AI agents to streamline tasks such as store setup, product listing, multilingual content management and data analysis, the brand increased regional orders by 30 percent and average order value by 22 percent over three months. Wang said another example is JammyJem, a Chinese brand selling squishy toys and blind-box products. "It uses online livestreams and TikTok short videos to engage overseas consumers, and buyers also share their purchases and unboxing videos, drawing in new shoppers," he said. JammyJem's data for Japan showed that around 60 percent of its customers who placed orders in a given month made at least two purchases that month, while about one-third placed orders five or more times. Rizzo, the Italian student, said her interest in Chinese products continues after she returns to Italy. She typically selects items on Taobao, Tmall and JD.com before traveling and has them delivered to an address in China. She tried ordering from China to Italy once but found international shipping expensive, particularly when buying from multiple sellers. Charl Albertyn is a 34-year-old South African who has lived in China since 2014. Through his company, Hofmeyr Consulting, he organizes trips for international visitors, while his work with Lumiverse Media LLC focuses on Chinese business, technology, food and consumer culture. Albertyn said his perception of Chinese brands had changed considerably over the years. He has witnessed Chinese companies grow stronger, not only in manufacturing, but also in design, technology, branding and consumer experience. "I don't think price is necessarily the most important attraction anymore," he said. "Chinese products can be attractive because of their quality, design, variety and technological innovation, but perhaps most importantly because they increasingly offer something that is distinctly Chinese." He sees this as part of a broader shift in China's global image. "After living here for more than a decade, that is probably the biggest change I have seen: China has moved from being perceived primarily as the world's factory to increasingly being recognized as a source of brands, products, experiences and ideas in its own right," said Albertyn. item.title: Global South delegates seek stronger voice at World Media Summit in Beijing
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Global South delegates seek stronger voice at World Media Summit in Beijing BEIJING, Nov. 8 (Xinhua) -- Senior media professionals from the Global South have called for closer cooperation at the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing to give their countries a stronger voice in global coverage as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the industry. Co-organized by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government, this year's summit runs from Nov. 5 to 9. It has drawn nearly 500 representatives of media outlets, think tanks and government bodies from 112 countries and regions, as well as the United Nations and other international organizations. Initiated in 2009, the World Media Summit has become a major platform for exchange and cooperation among media leaders and professionals across regions and language communities. "What is important about the summit is that it brings media outlets from around the world and gives us a forum to discuss the future of our industry," said Kenedid Ibrahim Houssein, director of publication of La Nation in Djibouti, who is attending the summit for the first time. "We hope to further develop partnership with China on information sharing based on this platform," he added. Ghislain Ruffin Etoughet Nzuet, chairman of the board of directors at Gabon Broadcasting Corporation, said the World Media Summit provides a platform for African countries to tell their own stories and speak for themselves. "Africa has a long tradition and a long history, yet very little is known about us," Nzuet said, adding that cooperation with partners around the world, particularly China, could help bring African perspectives into global discussions. Agnes Kalekye Nguna, managing director and CEO of Kenya Broadcasting Corporation, stressed the importance of dialogue among civilizations on an equal footing. She called for more initiatives to expand exchanges and deepen media cooperation between Africa and China, saying a partnership that benefits both sides could inspire similar efforts elsewhere in the Global South and beyond. Under this year's theme, "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action," delegates are also discussing how Global South countries could work together to help their media organizations adapt as AI use expands across the industry. "How do we ensure smaller nations have a meaningful voice in shaping the future of AI?" asked Aminath Namza, chairperson of Public Service Media in the Maldives, during discussions at the summit. She said many AI models are trained on data drawn mainly from societies with a greater digital presence, and therefore may not be able to fully reflect the languages, cultures and realities of smaller nations. "International cooperation must therefore ensure that developing countries and small island states can contribute not only to AI's development, but also to the principles governing it," she said. On Saturday, the 7th World Media Summit released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards. Launched by Xinhua, the initiative brings together major media outlets and other professional organizations to safeguard the authenticity of information, protect data security, and uphold media ethics, thereby maintaining public trust in the media. Under this initiative, participants plan to work together for about two years to develop a set of standards that address different media uses of AI and are validated by media outlets. Najeh Missaoui, director general and CEO of Tunis Afrique Presse, one of the first participants, regards the initiative as a major step forward. "It takes us from talking about AI to taking joint action and setting rules." "For us at Tunis Afrique Presse, this plan ensures that the Global South will have a hand in shaping the rules for AI, rather than simply consuming technology developed by others," he said. "We hope the initiative will become a practical avenue for cooperation, sharing expertise and building capacity, and media organizations of different sizes and with different resources can apply the standards," said Mohammed Alyami, director general of the Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, which is also among the first participants, in an interview with Xinhua. Wong Chun Wai, chairman of the Malaysian National News Agency (Bernama), said that, instead of access to basic AI tools, media organizations need to invest in advanced tools and train staff to use them effectively. He called on Global South countries to work together more closely in the changing media landscape and ensure that media organizations worldwide can share in the benefits of AI. Adopted at the summit on Saturday, the 7th World Media Summit Beijing Consensus calls for joint efforts to advance the transformation and development of the global media industry in the AI era. It commits to advancing the inclusive and responsible application of AI in the media sector so that advances in AI benefit media organizations at all stages of development and in every country. "The future of global communication must be intelligent, but above all, inclusive," said Viasen Soobramoney, CEO of South Africa's Independent Media IOL and the African News Agency, during the summit. Soobramoney called for transparent, accountable and inclusive global AI governance to help prevent the technology from reinforcing inequalities that have long affected many Global South countries. Africa and China could deepen cooperation in AI-assisted translation, multimedia production, journalist training, content verification and the exchange of technical expertise, he said. Abdul Hakim, president director of Indonesia's Antara News Agency, suggested closer cooperation on information sharing and verification, more exchanges on responsible AI use and newsroom innovation, and better coordination in reporting on global challenges. "No country, no community, and no voice should be left behind," he said. "This is why international cooperation matters so much." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China extends suspension of 24 pct additional tariff on U.S. goods for two months
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
China extends suspension of 24 pct additional tariff on U.S. goods for two months BEIJING, Nov. 9 (Xinhua) -- China will continue to suspend the 24 percent additional tariff rate on imports originating in the United States for two months while keeping the 10 percent additional tariff rate in place, according to the Customs Tariff Commission of the State Council on Monday. The adjustment, effective from 1:01 p.m. on Nov. 10, implements the outcomes and consensus reached at the meeting between the Chinese and U.S. heads of state in Washington, the commission said in an online statement. The move adjusts the additional tariff measures stipulated in the Announcement of the Customs Tariff Commission of the State Council No. 4 of 2025, in accordance with the country's tariff law, customs law and foreign trade law, as well as basic principles of international law. China has noted that the U.S. side has repeatedly stated its intention to replace the tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which have been ruled invalid, with Section 301 tariffs, said the commission. China will continue to closely follow the U.S. side's subsequent moves and adjust its relevant tariff countermeasures in light of the situation, the commission said. The continued suspension of part of the additional tariffs on U.S. imports is conducive to providing a relatively stable and predictable policy environment for cooperation between enterprises of both countries and to promoting the sustained and steady development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, it added. item.title: Beyond market size, European firms tap China's growth, innovation potential
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Beyond market size, European firms tap China's growth, innovation potential SHANGHAI, Nov. 8 (Xinhua) -- Amid dazzling displays at the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), a truck-sized turn-mill machine stands quietly, its computer-controlled spindle whirring. Without flashy decorations, the machine still draws curious crowds. The attraction is a piece of precision machinery from an Austrian "hidden champion" WFL, shown under the expo's "deep-tech" label. Weighing over 20 tonnes, the machine began its journey in August, crossing oceans and moving between trucks and shipping containers before arriving at the Port of Shanghai, host city of the CIIE -- a major platform for China to open its vast market to the world. Why go to such lengths? Mayr Günther Franz Josef, general manager of WFL, told Xinhua that participating in the CIIE offers a chance to gain firsthand insights into China's rapidly upgrading high-end manufacturing sector and to forge closer ties with industrial partners across the Asia-Pacific region. The company had another goal in mind: to make the machine's journey a one-way trip. As hoped, it found a buyer just three days into the expo. Across the exhibition floor, European companies are deepening their engagement with China, drawn not only by the sheer size of its market but increasingly by opportunities arising from industrial upgrading, evolving consumer demand and a vibrant innovation ecosystem. MORE THAN A VAST MARKET China's pursuit of high-quality development, coupled with rising living standards, has fueled increasingly sophisticated demand for industrial and consumer products, opening up new avenues of growth for businesses worldwide. "As China's manufacturing capabilities continue to advance, demand for high-end machine tools and other sophisticated industrial equipment is growing," said Zheng Xiaoli, a representative at WFL's booth. The company's machine tools are used to manufacture complex, high-precision components for industries including aviation, aerospace and shipbuilding. The changing composition of their Chinese clientele offers a glimpse into that transformation. "Our customers in China used to be mainly state-owned enterprises and foreign-invested companies. Now, a growing number of private Chinese manufacturers seeking quality products are investing in our high-end machinery," said Zheng. China's accelerating green transition and digital transformation are also creating fresh opportunities for European suppliers of advanced technologies and specialized materials. For AMORNEX, a joint venture between Luxembourg-based steelmaker ArcelorMittal and China Oriental Group, the booming electric vehicle industry in China is driving demand for advanced materials. Jurgen Cobbaut, the company's chief marketing officer, told Xinhua that some high-performance electric motors in Chinese EVs require materials with exceptional strength and efficiency, which plays to the company's strengths. "It's not only the volume, but also the level of sophistication. That is what really makes it interesting," Cobbaut said of the Chinese market. The shift toward more sophisticated demand extends to consumer markets, where changing lifestyles and rising expectations are also inspiring product innovation. German cleaning equipment manufacturer Kärcher, for example, developed a compact, foldable pressure washer for cleaning bicycles, cars and camping gear, tapping into Chinese consumers' growing enthusiasm for outdoor activities. Originally designed for the Chinese market, the product has since been rolled out globally. "Chinese consumers today are much more sophisticated. They're looking for products that fit their lifestyles," said Bernd Rützler, an executive vice president of Alfred Kärcher GmbH & Co. KG. INNOVATION ENGINE Beyond evolving demand, China's innovation capabilities, underpinned by its extensive supply chains and fast-evolving market, are becoming powerful draws for European companies. "China has always been one of our most important strategic markets globally. What has changed is the increasingly multifaceted role China plays," said Liu Ling, chief region leader of Philips China. For the Dutch health technology company, China is not only its second-largest market worldwide but also a "key supply-chain hub and engine of innovation." Increasingly, innovations developed in China are also finding their way into European companies' global product portfolios. Drawing on China's "strong industrial foundation, abundant innovation resources and diverse use cases," Schneider Electric has worked with Chinese partners to develop a range of proven, scalable solutions that are helping businesses across sectors become smarter, more efficient and greener, said Yin Zheng, executive vice president of China & East Asia Operations of Schneider Electric. In the medical equipment hall at the CIIE, widely regarded as one of the expo's most competitive sections, Swedish medical equipment manufacturer Elekta is showcasing its AI-powered AutoART adaptive radiotherapy solution. The system can shorten the adaptive radiotherapy process -- from imaging and treatment planning to treatment delivery -- to just 10 to 15 minutes. Developed in response to the demands of China's busy radiotherapy departments, this technology is intended for wider international use, according to Jin Jianxue, vice president and medical affairs director of Elekta China. COMPLEMENTARY STRENGTHS The CIIE offers a timely view of deepening business ties between China and Europe, as EU policymakers weigh trade issues with China. The deeper ties are rooted in strong complementarity between the two sides, said Shen Yi, an international relations scholar at Fudan University. As China seeks to upgrade its industries and improve living standards, it needs European products and expertise in areas such as advanced equipment, precision instruments, pharmaceuticals and professional services, Shen told Xinhua. Europe, in turn, stands to benefit from China's vast market, manufacturing capabilities and technological advances in sectors like batteries and solar power, he added. Illustrating such complementarity, Zhang Shuo, chief representative at the Beijing Representative Office of the Brussels-based European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA), noted that Europe's century-old automotive industry has deep expertise in engineering, safety and environmental technologies, while China has taken the lead in batteries and electric mobility. Cooperation is also moving beyond the traditional model of importing finished vehicles or transferring technology toward closer integration of industrial supply chains and joint research and development, he told Xinhua at their booth. ACEA is attending this year's CIIE as an exhibitor for the first time, although its member companies have long been regular participants. Going forward, China has called for an "upward balance" in trade, achieved through greater openness and an expanding economic pie, rather than a "downward balance" caused by closing markets. Ultimately, openness remains a powerful draw. As Rützler put it: "We see China as a reliable market and a reliable partner. Its continued opening up gives us the confidence to invest more." item.title: Xi congratulates Iotova on election as Bulgarian president
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Xi congratulates Iotova on election as Bulgarian president BEIJING, Nov. 9 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has extended congratulations to Iliana Iotova on her election as president of Bulgaria. In a message on Friday, Xi noted that Bulgaria was the second country in the world to establish diplomatic ties with the People's Republic of China, and that mutual respect, equality, and mutual benefit and win-win results have been hallmarks of the bilateral relations. In recent years, the two countries have been steadily advancing exchanges and cooperation at all levels and across all fields, while their strategic partnership has continued to deepen, said Xi. Xi also said that he attaches great importance to the development of the China-Bulgaria ties. He pledged to work with Iotova to guide the two countries as they march together along their respective paths to development and revitalization, build an even more positive, practical and dynamic bilateral relationship, and thereby bring greater benefits to the two peoples. item.title: Consumer goods at 9th CIIE reflect global trends
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09

item.title: How Xi steers China's green transformation and global climate action
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
How Xi steers China's green transformation and global climate action Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, plants a tree during a voluntary tree-planting activity at Baishan Town in Changping District of Beijing, capital of China, March 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Yan Yan) BEIJING, Nov. 9 (Xinhua) -- In 2026, the intensifying fallout of global climate change -- manifesting in catastrophic flooding, rampant wildfires, and record heatwaves -- reaffirms the imperative for immediate, coordinated global action. With global climate tipping points looming, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), set to kick off on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, will offer a new opportunity for the international community to renew momentum for more effective global climate cooperation. Under the leadership of President Xi Jinping, China has over the years stayed committed to advancing ecological protection and green transition domestically, and promoting international climate cooperation, making major global contributions to the world's fight against what many regard as an existential threat to humanity. "LIKE WE PROTECT OUR EYES" "We should protect the environment like we protect our eyes." This evocative principle -- voiced on various occasions by Xi -- frames ecological conservation not merely as a policy choice, but as a vital imperative drawn directly from his own experiences. "Over four decades ago, I lived and worked for many years in a small village on the Loess Plateau in western China," Xi recalled in reply to a letter from student representatives of the Global Alliance of Universities on Climate in 2020. Back then, the ecology and environment there was seriously damaged due to over-development, and the local people were trapped in poverty as a result. That experience has taught him that man and nature are a community of life and that the damage done to nature will ultimately hurt humanity. An avid reader of Chinese classics, Xi has also been deeply influenced by the traditional Chinese philosophy that views man as an integral part of nature. "All beings flourish when they live in harmony and receive nourishment from nature," he has said. This conviction underpins the signature environmental doctrine that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets," which Xi first introduced in 2005 while serving as Party chief of east China's Zhejiang Province. Upon becoming General Secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee in 2012, Xi made ecological conservation a national priority. An aerial drone photo taken on June 3, 2024 shows the scenery of the Fenhe River in Taiyuan, north China's Shanxi Province. (Xinhua/Yang Chenguang) For Xi, ecological conservation requires not only a profound shift in development philosophy, but also robust institutional safeguards. As he has put it, "Eco-environmental protection relies on laws and regulations." At his direction, environmental performance has become a key criterion for evaluating officials, while environmental inspections have reinforced local governments' accountability for fulfilling their environmental responsibilities. Together, these measures have helped steer China's economic growth toward a more resource-efficient and sustainable path. Since 2012, China has sustained a 6 percent average annual economic growth rate while capping an average energy consumption increase to just 3.3 percent. This structural decoupling yielded a 26.1 percent cumulative decline in energy intensity, marking one of the steepest efficiency gains globally. Xi has also led by example in promoting environmental protection and green development. Since becoming China's top leader, he has personally participated in tree-planting activities in Beijing for 14 consecutive years. Forests have the capacity to conserve water, bring in economic benefits, and boost grain production, and now serve well as a carbon sink, he has noted. Today, China has expanded its forest coverage to over 25 percent of its land area, planting trees across an area roughly 1.7 times the size of California since 2012. The annual carbon-sink capacity of China's forests and grassland has exceeded 1.2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents. Fuad Gani, vice director of the Graduate School of Sustainable Development at the University of Indonesia, said that China's ecological conservation philosophy stands out for its ability to translate environmental goals into long-term policies and governance frameworks. "It is one of China's most valuable contributions to advancing green transformation on the global stage," he said. An aerial drone photo taken on July 29, 2025 shows photovoltaic panels at the site of a desertification control project integrated with wind and solar power facilities in Horqin Right Wing Middle Banner of Hinggan League, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Ding He) "SOMETHING WE MUST DO OURSELVES" Balancing economic growth with green development remains a challenge for economies worldwide, especially emerging markets seeking to meet development needs while pursuing environmental sustainability. In Xi's view, economic growth and the green transition are not opposing forces, but complementary goals. This philosophy is captured in his defining doctrine -- "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets." Achieving China's carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals, Xi has stressed, "is not something that others ask us to do, but something we must do ourselves." Under his leadership, China has effectively aligned emissions reduction with technological innovation, industrial upgrading and energy security, turning the green transition into an increasingly important driver of high-quality development. As early as 2014, when conventional gasoline-powered vehicles still dominated China's roads, Xi recognized the enormous potential of new energy vehicles (NEVs). During an inspection tour of SAIC Motor, a major Chinese carmaker, Xi depicted developing NEVs as the only way for China to move from a major automobile country to an automobile powerhouse. In the following decade, the president has demonstrated consistent support for electric cars, visiting automotive companies, touring laboratories, and showing great interest in trying new home-developed models. China's NEV industry has since grown rapidly, emerging as a flagship of the country's technology-intensive manufacturing sector. Beyond the NEV sector, China has also built the world's largest and most comprehensive clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries emerging as an important engine of economic growth. The growing exports of the "new three" -- photovoltaic products, lithium-ion batteries and electric vehicles -- are a testament to China's successful shift toward innovation-driven manufacturing. Beyond its own borders, China is now channeling this green innovation momentum into regional cooperation. Customers view a Chinese-brand electric car in Jakarta, Indonesia, June 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng) China will continue to work with fellow Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) countries to increase the installed capacity of photovoltaic and wind power each by 10 million kilowatts, and nurture more green industry talents through China-SCO cooperation, said Xi at the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO this September. China's exports of solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries this year will help the world to avoid 450 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, according to a recent analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The development exemplifies China's strategic push to cultivate "new quality productive forces" -- a policy concept first articulated by Xi in 2023 to drive high-tech innovation and sustainable economic modernization. "Green development," as Xi once put it, "is the defining feature of high-quality development, and new quality productive forces are green in nature." China has turned the challenges of addressing climate change into opportunities for technological innovation, industrial upgrading and high-quality economic development, said Wang Lei, a professor at the School of Government of Beijing Normal University. "Guided by the goals of reducing carbon emissions and strengthening climate resilience, the country has leveraged policy guidance, market incentives and open innovation to drive the transformation of energy, industry, transportation and construction," he added. Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers a speech at the opening ceremony of the United Nations (UN) climate change conference in Paris, France, Nov. 30, 2015. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) "EXTREME RESOLUTIONS" Deeply committed to joining world nations to build a community with a shared future for humanity, Xi has repeatedly called on the international community to strengthen cooperation in addressing climate change and actively advanced the building of a fair and equitable global climate governance system for win-win cooperation. "Supreme resources spring from extreme resolutions," Xi said, invoking a perceptive line from French writer Victor Hugo's Les Miserables during his address to the historic 2015 Paris climate change conference. During the summit, Xi put forward important ideas and proposals and worked actively to build consensus among parties, making an indispensable contribution to the eventual adoption of the Paris Agreement. At a special ceremony on Sept. 3, 2016, Xi solemnly handed over China's instrument of joining the Paris Agreement to then UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon. "Had not been President Xi Jinping's initiative, we would not have the Paris Agreement on climate change even now," Ban said in a 2021 interview with Xinhua. In response to the grave challenge of climate change, China has taken on its international responsibilities with what Xi described as "extreme resolutions." At a virtual UN gathering in 2020, Xi announced that China would strive to peak carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality before 2060. In 2021, he pledged that China would not build new coal-fired power projects abroad. In recent years, some developed countries, particularly those in the West, have backtracked on their climate commitments, undermining global climate governance. Against this backdrop, Xi announced China's 2035 Nationally Determined Contributions in 2025, including a commitment to reduce economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions by 7-10 percent from peak levels and to raise the share of non-fossil fuels in total energy consumption to more than 30 percent by 2035. For the first time, China committed to absolute emissions reduction targets covering all economic sectors and all greenhouse gases, providing much-needed certainty and stability for global climate governance. Xi has also emphasized the need to uphold fairness and equity and fully respect developing countries' right to development as the world pursues a green transition. "The transition should serve to narrow rather than widen the North-South gap," he said, urging developed countries to take the lead in fulfilling emissions reduction obligations and provide more financial and technological support to developing countries. Under Xi's leadership, China has been striving to strengthen South-South cooperation on climate change. Xi has proposed the establishment of the Belt and Road Initiative International Green Development Coalition and advocated building a green BRICS partnership. Through these target-driven initiatives, China seeks to deepen cooperation in clean energy, green technology and green industrial development, while helping developing countries strengthen their capacity to address climate change. "The Earth is our one and only home," Xi has said. "To scale up efforts to address climate change and promote sustainable development bears on the future of humanity."
